subject: The Papyrus · The sport Egypt quietly owns
html:
Not football — squash

Egypt is famous for football, but there's a sport it doesn't just compete in — it dominates. In men's squash, an Egyptian has won the World Championship roughly 14 times since 2003, and Egyptians routinely fill the top of the world rankings for both men and women. It is one of the most complete national dominances in any global sport. (Sources: US Squash; Olympics.com.)

A wall of champions

The names run deep: Amr Shabana (4 world opens, Egypt's first world champion), Ramy Ashour (3 titles, once considered the most gifted player alive), Ali Farag (4 titles), and on the women's side Nour El Sherbini — 8 World Championships, equalling the all-time record. In 2024–25, Mostafa Asal won the men's world title without dropping a single game — a feat not managed since Jahangir Khan in 1988. (Source: US Squash, 2025.)

Why does one country produce so many? A dense club culture in Cairo and Alexandria, a coaching lineage that passes technique down, and juniors who grow up playing the best in the world in their own neighbourhoods. Dominance, when you look closely, is rarely a mystery — it's a system. Count the titles and the pattern is undeniable.
